name: Certified Implementation Specialist – Third-party Risk Management
note: ServiceNow does not publish a cut score for CIS-TPRM; community consensus puts it near 70%. Treat 85% here as your readiness bar. Items marked release-sensitive reference table names and labels that shift between releases.

questions.stem: A bank uses the same cloud provider for two things: hosting a marketing microsite, and processing customer payment data. Risk leadership wants the payment relationship assessed far more rigorously than the microsite, but wants one consolidated view of the provider. What should the implementation use?
options: Two separate third-party company records, one per service
One third-party record with two IRQ responses attached directly to the company
One third-party record with two engagements
One third-party record flagged as high criticality, with a single deep assessment covering both services
questions.explanation:
The engagement is the unit of service-level risk. It lets the same third party carry different inherent risk, different tiers, and different due-diligence scope per relationship while rolling up to one portfolio record.

Two company records fragment monitoring, contacts, and reporting — the exact problem engagements were introduced to solve. Attaching two IRQ responses to the company with no engagement gives you no object to scope the assessments to. Assessing both services at the payment tier wastes assessor capacity and inflates the provider's apparent risk.

questions.stem: Who is the intended respondent for a third-party Inherent Risk Questionnaire (IRQ)?
options: The assigned third-party risk assessor, during review
The third party's designated information security officer
The third party's primary contact, responding through the portal
The internal business owner sponsoring the relationship
questions.explanation:
The IRQ is internal. It asks what the business intends to do with this third party — what data they touch, whether they connect to the network, whether the service is business-critical — and the business owner is the only person who knows. The third party is not asked to rate its own inherent risk.

This is one of the most reliably tested distinctions on the exam: IRQ/tiering is internal, risk assessments go outward to the third party.

questions.stem: What does the tiering process determine?
options: The third party's contractual service level
The external security rating pulled from a risk intelligence provider
Residual risk remaining after the third party's controls are verified
Inherent risk, which sets the depth and scope of due diligence
questions.explanation:
Tiering measures inherent risk — the risk the relationship carries before any control is considered — and that tier drives how much due diligence is warranted.

Residual risk is only knowable after assessment responses and control evidence are reviewed, so it cannot be an input to scoping. Contractual service levels and external ratings are separate signals; neither defines the tier.

questions.stem: Put the core TPRM lifecycle in the order the application supports it.
options: Intake → tiering → due diligence assessment → contracting → ongoing monitoring → offboarding
Due diligence assessment → intake → tiering → contracting → monitoring → offboarding
Tiering → intake → contracting → due diligence assessment → monitoring → offboarding
Intake → due diligence assessment → tiering → monitoring → contracting → offboarding
questions.explanation:
Intake captures the request and the third party, tiering establishes inherent risk, due diligence tests controls proportionate to that tier, contracting locks in obligations informed by findings, monitoring watches for change, and offboarding closes the relationship out.

The sequencing trap is putting assessment before tiering. If you assess first you have no basis for deciding how deep to assess.

questions.stem: Select two outcomes that follow directly from completing and approving tiering. (Choose two.)
options: The third party's contract is generated and routed for signature
A residual risk score is calculated for the engagement
Applicable due-diligence assessments are triggered based on the responses
An inherent risk tier is assigned to the third party or engagement
questions.explanation:
Tiering produces the tier, and the tier plus specific IRQ answers drive which assessments get generated — a data-privacy answer pulls in a privacy questionnaire, a network-connectivity answer pulls in a security questionnaire.

Residual risk requires completed assessments. Contract generation is downstream and is not an automatic product of tiering.

questions.stem: A user needs to review submitted third-party responses, score them, and raise issues — but must not be able to configure questionnaires or change program settings. Which role fits?
options: Third-party risk assessor
Third-party risk reader
Third-party risk manager
Third-party user (portal)
questions.explanation:
The assessor works the assessment queue: reviews responses, evaluates evidence, scores, and raises issues. The manager owns program configuration and oversight, which is more than this user needs. The reader is view-only and cannot score. The third-party user is the external respondent and has no internal visibility at all.

Least privilege is the reasoning pattern the exam rewards here — pick the narrowest role that still does the job.

questions.stem: Why does the program run continuous or external monitoring alongside periodic reassessment?
options: It replaces questionnaire-based assessment entirely for lower-tier third parties
It satisfies the contract's right-to-audit clause without any further review
It surfaces changes in a third party's posture between scheduled reassessments
It calculates each engagement's inherent risk tier automatically from ratings
questions.explanation:
A point-in-time questionnaire goes stale the moment it is submitted. Monitoring — breach news, external security ratings, financial and sanctions signals — is what tells you something changed in month four of a twelve-month cycle.

It supplements rather than replaces assessments, because outside-in signal says nothing about internal control design. It does not set the tier, and it is not a substitute for exercising an audit right.

questions.stem: What changed conceptually when Vendor Risk Management became Third-party Risk Management?
options: Third parties stopped being represented as company records on the platform
Assessments moved from the Assessment framework into Flow Designer subflows
Scope widened beyond purchased goods to any external party creating exposure
Tiering became an optional step that programs could skip for most vendors
questions.explanation:
"Vendor" implies a purchasing relationship. "Third party" covers resellers, agents, brokers, joint-venture partners, contract researchers, and other parties who create exposure without ever sending an invoice — which is how regulators frame the obligation.

The underlying assessment framework, the company-record foundation, and the centrality of tiering all carried forward unchanged.

questions.stem: Risk leadership wants to see where its active third parties and engagements are physically located, to spot geographic concentration. Which capability addresses this?
options: The assessment heat grid
The CMDB dependency map
The engagement Gantt view
The risk concentration map
questions.explanation:
Concentration risk — too many critical engagements in one country, one region, or one provider — is a board-level TPRM question, and the concentration map plots active third parties and engagements geographically to expose it.

Gantt views belong to project management, dependency maps to the CMDB, and assessment scoring grids show risk level rather than location.

questions.stem: An executive asks for a third party's overall risk position across all of its engagements. Where does that come from?
options: A roll-up on the third-party record of engagement results and monitoring
The IRQ response for whichever engagement has the largest contract value
The most recent single assessment score from any one of its engagements
The average tier across all of the contacts registered for the third party
questions.explanation:
Engagement-level results roll up to the third-party record, which is what gives you an entity view across every service that party provides, plus external monitoring.

A single assessment is one service at one point in time. One engagement's IRQ ignores the rest of the portfolio. Contacts carry no tier at all.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between inherent and residual risk in a TPRM assessment cycle?
options: Inherent risk is calculated from assessment responses; residual risk comes from the IRQ
Residual risk is always lower than inherent risk once any assessment has been closed
Inherent risk is exposure before controls; residual is what remains after controls are evaluated
They are the same measure, captured at two different points in the assessment cycle
questions.explanation:
Inherent comes from the IRQ and describes what the relationship exposes you to. Residual is derived from the assessed control environment.

Deriving inherent risk from assessment responses and residual risk from the IRQ inverts the sources. Residual is not guaranteed to land lower — a third party with weak controls can end up at or above its inherent position, and that is precisely the finding the process exists to surface.

questions.stem: Select two reasons to assess at the engagement level rather than only at the third-party level. (Choose two.)
options: Engagements allow separate reassessment cadence per service
Only engagements can hold third-party contacts
Engagements are required before a company record can be created
Different services from the same provider carry different data sensitivity
questions.explanation:
Data sensitivity and criticality vary by service, and each engagement can therefore carry its own tier, scope, and reassessment schedule.

The third-party record exists independently — you create the party, then the engagements under it. Contacts belong to the third party, not to the engagement.

questions.stem: A relationship is being terminated. Which action belongs in offboarding?
options: Move the third party to the lowest tier and leave its record active indefinitely
Close or cancel open assessments and issues, and revoke portal access
Generate a fresh full-scope risk assessment to document the vendor's final state
Delete the third-party company record along with its assessment history
questions.explanation:
Offboarding is about closing out work in flight and cutting access. Portal access left live after termination is a standing audit finding.

Deleting the record destroys the evidence trail you are required to retain. Demoting the tier while leaving it active misrepresents the portfolio. A new full assessment at exit is wasted effort — the point is exit, not evaluation.

questions.stem: What is the practical function of third-party criticality within the program?
options: It is calculated automatically from the number of engagements
It helps drive prioritization, assessment depth, and monitoring intensity
It replaces the inherent risk tier for regulated third parties
It determines which portal theme the third party sees
questions.explanation:
Criticality — how badly the business is hurt if this party fails — works alongside inherent risk to decide who gets attention first and how much of it.

It is a business judgment, not a count of engagements, and it complements rather than replaces the tier. Portal theming is unrelated.

questions.stem: A global third party operates through several regional subsidiaries, each contracted separately. Reporting must show both the subsidiaries and consolidated parent exposure. How should the portfolio be configured?
options: Parent and child company records related through the company hierarchy
One flat company record with the subsidiaries listed in a description field
One company record per subsidiary with no relationship between them
Separate engagements standing in for each subsidiary
questions.explanation:
The company hierarchy is what produces consolidated parent exposure while keeping each contracting entity assessable on its own.

Flat records and unrelated records both lose the roll-up. Engagements describe services, not legal entities — using them for corporate structure breaks down the moment a subsidiary provides more than one service.

questions.stem: Select two conditions that must be true for a third-party contact to receive and respond to an assessment. (Choose two.)
options: The contact has been granted the third-party portal role
The contact has an active user record associated with the third-party company
The contact is designated as the primary contact
The contact has been added to the internal assessor group
questions.explanation:
Respondents need an identity the platform recognizes and the portal entitlement that lets them in. That is the whole requirement.

Primary contact is a designation for default routing and correspondence, not a precondition for responding — any entitled contact can be a respondent. Adding an external party to an internal assessor group would give them visibility into other third parties' data.

questions.stem: What does third-party risk intelligence scoring contribute that questionnaires do not?
options: Verified evidence of how the third party's internal controls are designed
A legally binding attestation from the third party about its security controls
Continuously refreshed outside-in signal about the third party's posture
The engagement's inherent risk tier, calculated directly from the rating
questions.explanation:
Risk intelligence providers observe a third party from the outside — exposed infrastructure, breach disclosures, financial and sanctions signals — and refresh continuously. That is change detection between cycles.

It cannot see inside a control environment, carries no attestation weight, and does not set the tier. Questionnaires and intelligence answer different questions; the exam tests that you know which is which.

questions.stem: A third party's external security rating drops below the configured threshold. What is the appropriate configured response?
options: Automatically terminate the engagement as soon as the rating falls below the threshold
Recalculate the engagement's inherent risk tier directly from the new external score
Suspend the third party's portal access until an assessor has reviewed the drop
Trigger a defined action, such as raising an issue or starting a reassessment
questions.explanation:
Thresholds exist to convert a signal into work. The configured response is an issue for investigation or an out-of-cycle assessment, with a human deciding what the drop actually means.

Automatic termination on a third-party rating is not a defensible control. External scores do not overwrite inherent risk, which is a function of what you use the party for. Cutting portal access removes the channel you need to ask them about it.

questions.stem: What is the primary contact designation used for?
options: It marks the contact as the third party's legal signatory for all contracts
It gives that contact admin rights over the company's other contacts and routing
It restricts assessment responses so that only that person can answer them
It determines the third party's inherent risk tier for every engagement
questions.explanation:
The primary contact is the default counterparty: correspondence routes there, and that contact typically manages the third party's other users on the portal.

It carries no legal signatory meaning, does not lock out other respondents, and has nothing to do with tiering.

questions.stem: Two teams have independently created records for the same supplier under slightly different names. What is the correct remediation?
options: Convert one of the records into an engagement underneath the other record
Consolidate onto one record using a unique identifier, and retire the duplicate
Delete both records and recreate a single new record for the supplier from scratch
Leave both records in place and filter reports so they use only the newer one
questions.explanation:
Duplicates split assessment history, monitoring, and contacts, so consolidation onto one authoritative record keyed to a unique identifier such as a D-U-N-S number is the fix.

Filtering hides the problem. Converting a company to an engagement destroys its own engagement structure. Deleting both throws away the history you need to keep.

questions.stem: During intake, where does the information that drives assessment scope originate?
options: The internal requester's answers about data, access, and criticality
The external risk intelligence feed that rates the third party's posture
The third party's own profile information, as entered through the portal
The procurement purchase order raised for the third party's services
questions.explanation:
Scope is set by what the business intends to do with the third party, captured from the internal requester at intake and formalized through tiering.

A portal profile is self-reported by the third party. A purchase order describes commercials. The intelligence feed arrives later and reflects posture, not intended use.

questions.stem: Third-party types are being configured for the portfolio. What is the design goal?
options: To give each type its own distinct portal login URL for the third parties in it
To classify parties so templates, workflows, and reporting apply by category
To determine which currency is used on contracts with each type of third party
To set the maximum number of contacts each third party is allowed to register
questions.explanation:
Typing is a routing and reporting construct: a staffing agency, a cloud processor, and a contract manufacturer warrant different questionnaires and different reporting cuts.

Portal URL, contact limits, and currency are unrelated to type classification.

questions.stem: TPRM questionnaires are built on which platform capability?
options: Knowledge Management article templates
Flow Designer subflows and actions
Service Catalog record producers
The Survey and Assessment framework
questions.explanation:
Questionnaires are assessment metrics organized into categories under a metric type, with templates assembling them. Understanding that lineage is what lets you troubleshoot scoring and question ordering.

Flow Designer orchestrates the process around assessments. Record producers create intake requests. Knowledge articles carry guidance, not scored questions.

questions.stem: Which table drives sending a specific risk assessment based on how a question on the IRQ was answered?
options: The metric category table for grouped questions
The assessment instance table for issued assessments
The question-to-assessment mapping table
The third-party engagement table for relationships
questions.explanation:
A many-to-many mapping between IRQ questions and assessments is what makes tiering adaptive: answer yes to "will they process personal data" and the privacy questionnaire is added to the due-diligence set.

Instance tables hold issued assessments. Metric categories group questions. The engagement table holds the relationship. None of them carry the trigger logic.

questions.stem: Select two valid ways a third-party risk assessment can be generated. (Choose two.)
options: By the third party, from the portal, whenever they choose
Automatically, from responses on a completed tiering questionnaire
By the CMDB discovery schedule
Manually, by a third-party risk manager or assessor
questions.explanation:
Assessments originate internally — automatically from tiering logic and scheduled reassessment, or manually when someone decides an out-of-cycle review is warranted.

A third party cannot commission its own assessment; that would let the assessed party control scope. Discovery has no role in TPRM assessment generation.

questions.stem: A third party submits its questionnaire. What state does the assessment move into next?
options: Draft, so the third party can keep editing
Closed complete, with the score calculated
Awaiting response from the third party
Under review by the assigned assessor
questions.explanation:
Submission ends the respondent's turn and starts the internal one. The assessor reviews answers and evidence, scores, and raises issues before anything closes.

Closing on submission would skip review entirely. Draft and awaiting-response are both upstream states.

questions.stem: A submitted assessment is missing the evidence attachments several answers depend on. What is the correct handling?
options: Score the affected questions as failures and close it complete
Return it to the third party for the missing information and keep it open
Close it incomplete and schedule an out-of-cycle reassessment
Raise an issue and accept the responses as submitted
questions.explanation:
Missing evidence is a gap in the response, not a finding about the control. Sending it back keeps the assessment record whole and puts the burden where it belongs.

Closing incomplete discards work already done. Scoring unverified answers as outright failures manufactures findings. Accepting unevidenced responses defeats the purpose of asking.

questions.stem: What distinguishes closed complete from closed incomplete?
options: Complete means it reached a scored result; incomplete means it ended without one
Complete means the third party passed; incomplete means the third party failed
Complete applies only to tiering; incomplete applies only to risk assessments
Complete means all issues are remediated; incomplete means some issues remain open
questions.explanation:
The distinction is about process completion, not outcome. A low-scoring assessment that was fully worked is closed complete. One abandoned because the engagement was cancelled or the third party never responded is closed incomplete.

Outstanding issues have their own lifecycle and do not hold the assessment open.

questions.stem: How do question weights affect a risk assessment result?
options: They control which questions are visible to the third party
They set each response's proportional contribution to the score
They set the order in which questions appear to the respondent
They define the due date for each response in the questionnaire
questions.explanation:
Weighting is how you make an encryption-at-rest answer count more than an office-hours answer. The score is the weighted aggregate of responses.

Order, visibility, and due dates are all configured elsewhere.

questions.stem: Several questions on a questionnaire gather context that should not move the score. How do you configure them?
options: Mark them optional
Remove them from the template and collect them by email
Configure them so they carry no scoring contribution
Place them in a separate category at the end
questions.explanation:
Set the contribution to zero and the question is asked, answered, and stored without distorting the result.

Email collection loses the audit trail. Optional controls whether an answer is required, not whether it scores. Category placement changes grouping only.

questions.stem: To what type of assessment record does a third-party contact respond?
options: The risk assessment issued to the third party
The external monitoring assessment from a ratings provider
The internal control attestation for the engagement
The tiering questionnaire for the engagement
questions.explanation:
Only the outward-facing risk assessment goes to the third party's contacts. Tiering is internal, attestations are answered by internal control owners, and external monitoring is machine-generated from provider data with no respondent at all.

This item is the same trap as the IRQ question, approached from the other side.

questions.stem: Select two factors typically considered in third-party risk assessment calculations. (Choose two.)
options: The length of the third party's company name
The third party's financial stability
The number of contacts registered on the portal
The third party's adherence to relevant industry standards and frameworks
questions.explanation:
Control maturity against recognized frameworks and financial viability are both standard inputs — a financially failing provider is an availability risk regardless of how good its security is.

Contact count and name length are noise. Distractor sets on this exam sometimes include one obviously absurd option; take the free elimination and focus on separating the two plausible remainders.

questions.stem: Reassessment cadence should vary by tier: tier 1 annually, tier 3 every three years. Where does this belong?
options: Hard-coded into each questionnaire template as a fixed frequency
Tracked manually by assessors on a shared team calendar each year
Configured as tier-driven reassessment scheduling in program setup
Set individually on each third-party contact record by the assessor
questions.explanation:
Cadence is program configuration keyed to tier, so it applies consistently and survives staff turnover.

Templates define content, not schedule. Manual calendars fail audit the first time someone leaves. Contacts are people, not schedules.

questions.stem: A questionnaire template is revised while forty assessments using it are still awaiting responses. What happens to those in-flight assessments?
options: They are cancelled and reissued automatically
They are held until an administrator republishes them
They continue against the version they were issued under
They immediately adopt the revised questions
questions.explanation:
Issued instances keep the content they were issued with. Changing questions mid-response would invalidate answers already given and break comparability with the responses being scored beside them.

If you need the new content in flight, you reissue deliberately — nothing cancels or republishes on its own.

questions.stem: A third-party respondent cannot answer the security questions and needs a colleague to handle that section. What does the application support?
options: The internal assessor answers those questions on the third party's behalf
Delegate the assessment, or sections of it, to another registered contact
The assessment is cancelled and reissued to the colleague from scratch
The respondent shares their login credentials with the colleague
questions.explanation:
Delegation to another registered contact of the same third party is designed in, because real questionnaires span security, legal, finance, and operations.

Credential sharing destroys attribution. Assessors answering on the respondent's behalf destroys independence. Cancel-and-reissue loses everything already answered.

questions.stem: A respondent completes half a long questionnaire and closes the browser. What should happen?
options: The assessment locks and requires assessor intervention
Progress is saved and the respondent resumes where they stopped
The assessment auto-submits with the answers given so far
Responses are discarded and the questionnaire restarts
questions.explanation:
Partial progress persists. Long questionnaires are answered across multiple sittings by multiple people, and any other behavior would make the portal unusable.

Auto-submitting partial work would push an incomplete response into review and corrupt the score.

questions.stem: An assessor disagrees with the score a third party's response produced and believes the control is weaker than claimed. What is the correct action?
options: Lower the third party's inherent risk tier to reflect the weaker control
Record the assessor's evaluation and rationale, leaving the response intact
Close the assessment incomplete and reissue it to the third party
Edit the third party's submitted answer so it reflects what's really in place
questions.explanation:
The respondent's answer is evidence of what they asserted and must stay as submitted. The assessor's judgment is recorded alongside it with rationale, which is what an auditor will want to see.

Editing submitted answers destroys the record. Reissuing punishes the third party for the assessor's disagreement. Tier reflects inherent risk and is not an assessment outcome.

questions.stem: A response indicates a control the organization requires is absent. What should the configuration produce?
options: Automatic closure of the whole assessment as failed, with no further review
A notification sent to the procurement team only, with no other follow-up
An issue raised against the third party or engagement to track remediation
An immediate drop in the third party's external security rating from the provider
questions.explanation:
Findings become issues, and issues carry owners, remediation plans, and due dates. That is the mechanism that converts assessment output into work.

Assessments do not fail closed on a single gap. Notification alone tracks nothing. External ratings come from providers and are not written by your instance.

questions.stem: Select two legitimate ways to reduce assessment burden on both sides. (Choose two.)
options: Let third parties choose which questions they answer
Reuse a still-current assessment result across engagements of comparable risk with the same party
Send every third party the full questionnaire and ignore low-tier responses
Scope questionnaire depth to the assessed tier
questions.explanation:
Tier-based scoping and controlled reuse of recent, comparable results are the two supported levers. Both preserve rigor where risk warrants it.

Sending everything and ignoring most of it wastes the third party's time and yours. Letting respondents self-select questions hands scope control to the assessed party.

questions.stem: Where does a third party attach supporting evidence such as a SOC 2 report?
options: As an attachment on the assessment or response, through the portal
By emailing it directly to the assigned assessor for safekeeping
By uploading it to the organization's internal document repository
Evidence isn't collected in TPRM; assessors take answers at face value
questions.explanation:
Evidence lands on the record it supports, through the portal, so it stays joined to the response an assessor is scoring.

Email breaks the audit trail and hides evidence in a mailbox. External parties have no access to internal repositories.

questions.stem: A regulator-driven change means a new question must be asked of all tier 1 third parties on their next cycle. What is the correct approach?
options: Create a parallel questionnaire with the new question and email it to vendors separately
Add it to the template for future assessments, and reissue only where it's needed sooner
Edit every in-flight assessment to insert the new question into what's already been sent
Wait for the next platform upgrade, which will add the regulator's question automatically
questions.explanation:
Template forward, targeted reissue where urgency demands it. In-flight edits invalidate responses already in progress, and a parallel emailed questionnaire lives outside scoring, reporting, and the evidence trail.

Nothing about this depends on an upgrade.

questions.stem: An assessment issued for an engagement should reflect that engagement only, not every service the third party provides. What ensures this?
options: The assessment is generated in the context of the engagement and scoped to it
The assessor manually deletes irrelevant questions after issuing
A separate third-party record is created per service
The third party is instructed in the covering email to answer for one service only
questions.explanation:
Scope comes from context at generation. The engagement it was raised against is what the assessment is about, and that context carries through to scoring and reporting.

Post-issue question deletion breaks comparability. An instruction in an email is not a control. Duplicate company records reintroduce the fragmentation engagements exist to prevent.

questions.stem: Which set of activities is a third-party contact able to perform on the portal?
options: Approve their own remediation work and close their own issues when they're done
Respond to assessments, view project Gantt charts, and submit incidents for IT
View other third parties' benchmark scores and respond to their own assessments
Respond to assessments, manage their company's contacts, and view their issues
questions.explanation:
The portal gives the third party exactly what it needs to participate: answer, upload, manage its own people, and see its own findings.

Gantt charts and incident submission belong to other applications. Cross-party visibility would be a data breach. Self-approval of remediation removes the entire point of the control.

questions.stem: A third-party contact logs into the portal successfully but sees no assessments. What is the most likely cause?
options: The portal theme hasn't been published, so assessments are hidden from view
The contact's browser isn't supported, so the assessment list doesn't render
Nothing is assigned to the contact, or it's linked to the wrong company record
The assessment is still within its due date window, so it isn't shown yet
questions.explanation:
Successful login means authentication and the portal role are fine, so the problem is assignment or association — nothing is routed to them, or they are attached to a different company record than the one the assessment was issued against. Duplicate company records are a common root cause.

Theming would not block record visibility, and an open due date is exactly when the assessment should appear.

questions.stem: What prevents a third-party user from seeing another third party's data on the portal?
options: Access controls that scope visibility to the user's associated company
Assessments are delivered as read-only PDFs
The portal only displays records created in the last 90 days
Each third party gets its own instance
questions.explanation:
Company-scoped access control is the enforcement mechanism, evaluated per record.

Separate instances per third party would be unmanageable at any real portfolio size. Date filtering and PDF delivery are not access controls, and testing this isolation is a standard part of a TPRM go-live.

questions.stem: The organization wants the portal to carry its own branding rather than platform defaults. What is involved?
options: Configuring the portal's theme, logo, and styling
Rewriting the portal widgets in a custom scoped application
Branding is fixed and cannot be changed
Purchasing a separate portal license per third party
questions.explanation:
Theming is configuration — logo, colors, styling on the delivered portal.

Rewriting widgets is unnecessary custom work for a supported setting, per-party licensing is not how the portal works, and branding is certainly changeable.

questions.stem: Select two capabilities typically reserved for a third party's primary or administrative contact rather than every registered contact. (Choose two.)
options: Answering questions on an assigned assessment
Uploading evidence to a response
Adding and deactivating their company's other portal contacts
Receiving default correspondence and assessment notifications for the company
questions.explanation:
Managing the company's user roster and acting as the default correspondence point are administrative functions.

Answering and uploading are what every entitled respondent does — restricting them to one person would make multi-domain questionnaires impossible to complete.

questions.stem: Why does a third-party contact need an identity in the platform rather than an anonymous response link?
options: Anonymous links are technically unsupported by the assessment engine itself
Attribution, delegation, access control, and an auditable record of answers
So the contact can view the internal risk register for their own company
So the contact counts toward the organization's licensed user total
questions.explanation:
Every answer needs a name attached to it. An identity is also what makes delegation, partial save, and company-scoped access control work at all.

Third-party users never see the internal risk register, and licensing is not the design rationale.

questions.stem: A third party asks to see the score its assessment produced. What is the appropriate configuration decision?
options: Always expose the full internal scoring model and every assessor note to the vendor
Decide deliberately what to expose: findings usually, internal scoring usually not
Never share anything with the vendor, including the issues raised against it
Let each assessor decide case by case what to share with each third party
questions.explanation:
This is a policy decision made once and configured consistently. Third parties generally need to see what they must fix; they generally do not need the internal scoring model or assessor deliberations, which are often comparative across your portfolio.

Withholding issues makes remediation impossible. Per-assessor discretion produces inconsistent treatment that third parties will notice and challenge.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an approval step after the IRQ is completed?
options: To let the third party review and confirm the tier it has been assigned
To release the contract for signature once the tier has been calculated
To publish the questionnaire template that the third party will receive
To have risk management validate the tier and scope before due diligence
questions.explanation:
The IRQ is answered by a business owner with an interest in moving fast. The approval is the check that the resulting tier and due-diligence scope are defensible before assessments go out the door.

The third party has no say in its own tier. Contracting and template publishing are separate processes.

questions.stem: An IRQ approval is rejected. What should happen?
options: It returns to the requester for correction and resubmission
It is forwarded to the third party for comment
The third-party record is deactivated
The due-diligence assessments are issued anyway with a warning flag
questions.explanation:
Rejection sends it back to the person who answered it. The reviewer has judged the intake information wrong or incomplete, and the requester is the one who can fix it.

The third party is not part of the internal tiering loop. Proceeding anyway defeats the control, and deactivating the party over a questionnaire correction is wildly disproportionate.

questions.stem: Who should own remediation of an issue arising from a third party's missing control?
options: The third party, with an internal owner tracking and accepting the fix
The platform administrator, who configured the assessment that found it
Always the procurement team, since they manage the vendor contract
Always the internal risk assessor who identified the missing control
questions.explanation:
The third party has to fix its own control. Someone internal still owns chasing it, evaluating what comes back, and accepting or escalating — because the risk sits with your organization regardless of who performs the work.

Assessors evaluate rather than remediate on a third party's behalf, and administrators own the platform, not the finding.

questions.stem: Where is the orchestration behind onboarding, approvals, and assessment progression configured?
options: In a script include attached to each questionnaire template
In the portal theme and its widget configuration settings
In Flow Designer flows and the application's process configuration
In the assessment metric definitions for each questionnaire
questions.explanation:
Process orchestration lives in flows and process configuration, which is what makes it visible and maintainable by implementers rather than buried in script.

Metric definitions define questions. Themes control appearance. Scripting questionnaire-level orchestration is the anti-pattern this question is testing.

questions.stem: An assessment has passed its due date with no response. What should a well-configured program do?
options: Suspend the engagement until the third party submits its response
Close the assessment incomplete as soon as the due date passes
Escalate through reminders and notify the internal relationship owner
Automatically score every missing response as a failure and close it
questions.explanation:
Non-response is usually a contact problem — wrong person, someone who left, mail filtered. Escalation through reminders and the internal owner, who has the commercial relationship, resolves most of it.

Immediate closure, punitive scoring, and engagement suspension are all available as later escalation steps, not as the first automated move.

questions.stem: Select two conditions that should be satisfied before a third-party risk issue is closed. (Choose two.)
options: Remediation evidence has been provided and evaluated
The third party's external rating has improved
The next reassessment has been completed
A closure decision is recorded, whether remediated or formally accepted
questions.explanation:
Evidence evaluated and a recorded decision — remediated or risk accepted through the proper channel — are what closure requires.

External ratings move for reasons unrelated to your specific finding. Waiting for the next full reassessment would leave issues open for months or years.

questions.stem: Why route risk acceptance for an unremediated third-party finding through a formal approval?
options: It recalculates the third party's inherent risk tier automatically
It records who accepted the residual exposure and on what basis
It closes all of the third party's other open issues at the same time
It is required before the third party can access the portal again
questions.explanation:
Accepted risk is still risk. The approval names the accountable party and the rationale, which is exactly what an auditor or regulator asks for when the accepted risk later materializes.

Acceptance does not touch portal access, tiering, or other issues.

questions.stem: How do third parties connect to the wider GRC data model so their controls can be monitored alongside internal ones?
options: They are represented as configuration items in the CMDB
They are stored as knowledge articles
They exist only within the TPRM scoped application with no GRC linkage
They are represented as entities in the GRC entity and profile framework
questions.explanation:
Representing third parties as entities is what lets controls, risks, and policies attach to them, so third-party control performance appears in the same monitoring and reporting as everything else.

CIs describe technology assets. Keeping TPRM data isolated would defeat the point of running it on a GRC platform.

questions.stem: A third-party assessment surfaces a concentration exposure the enterprise risk team needs to own. What is the correct handling?
options: Reflect it in the risk register so it is governed alongside other enterprise risks
Convert the assessment into an audit engagement
Log it as a security incident
Leave it in TPRM — third-party risk is tracked separately from enterprise risk
questions.explanation:
Third-party risk is a category of enterprise risk, not a parallel universe. Material exposures belong in the register where they get owners, appetite comparison, and executive visibility.

Audit engagements and security incidents are different response paths for different triggers.

questions.stem: What does integration with contract management add to the TPRM process?
options: It assigns portal roles to third-party contacts named in the contract
It generates the inherent risk tier directly from the contract's total value
It ties obligations, renewals, and audit rights to the relationship assessed
It replaces the need for due-diligence assessments on contracted vendors
questions.explanation:
Assessment findings shape what goes into a contract, and contract terms — audit rights, notification obligations, renewal timing — shape what you can require later. Renewal is also a natural reassessment trigger.

Contracts do not substitute for assessment, contract value alone does not set inherent risk, and portal roles are managed in TPRM.

questions.stem: How does continuous control monitoring through indicators relate to third-party assessment?
options: Indicators give ongoing automated signal between point-in-time assessments
Indicators are only for internal controls and can't reference third parties
Indicators calculate the assessment score from the third party's responses
Indicators replace questionnaires for every tier once they're configured
questions.explanation:
Indicators test conditions on a schedule and surface drift without waiting for the next questionnaire. Point-in-time and continuous evidence answer different questions and are designed to run together.

They neither replace assessments nor compute their scores, and they can absolutely be pointed at third-party entities.

questions.stem: A cloud provider you use relies on a separate company to run its datacenters. What is that company to you?
options: Out of scope, because you have no contract with them
A fourth party, whose risk reaches you through your third party
A direct third party that you must contract with yourself
An internal business unit covered by your own policies
questions.explanation:
Fourth (or nth) parties are your third parties' own suppliers. You don't contract with them, but their failures can still disrupt you, so mature programs ask third parties about their critical subcontractors.

Treating them as out of scope ignores a real source of risk.

questions.stem: Why do regulators expect organizations to manage third-party risk?
options: Regulators want organizations to stop using third parties for any critical services
Third-party risk only matters if the vendor is based in a different country
Outsourcing a service doesn't transfer accountability for the risks that come with it
Third parties are legally required to manage all of the risk on the customer's behalf
questions.explanation:
You can outsource the work but not the accountability. If a provider mishandles data or fails, regulators hold the organization responsible.

Third parties don't absorb your obligations, regulators don't ban outsourcing, and domestic vendors carry risk too.

questions.stem: Which set lists common due-diligence domains in a third-party risk program?
options: Only the vendor's marketing materials and customer testimonials
Office décor, parking availability, and cafeteria quality at the vendor site
Only the vendor's price compared with competitors in the same market
Information security, privacy, financial health, compliance, and resilience
questions.explanation:
Due diligence covers the ways a third party can hurt you: security breaches, privacy violations, financial failure, regulatory problems, and service disruption.

Price comparisons and marketing are procurement concerns, not risk due diligence.

questions.stem: Which contract clauses most directly support ongoing third-party risk management?
options: Logo usage and marketing approval rights
Office hours and holiday schedule terms
Right to audit and breach notification obligations
Invoice formatting and payment address details
questions.explanation:
Audit rights let you verify controls after signing, and breach notification ensures you learn about incidents quickly. Both give the risk program something to enforce.

Branding, schedules, and invoicing are commercial details.

questions.stem: For a critical third party, why should an exit strategy be planned in advance?
options: So services can move to another provider or in-house without serious disruption
So the relationship can be ended quickly whenever an assessment finds an issue
Because regulators require every vendor contract to end after one year
Because exit plans replace the need for due diligence before onboarding
questions.explanation:
If a critical provider fails or must be replaced, a tested exit plan keeps the business running. Regulations such as DORA make this explicit for critical ICT providers.

Exit plans aren't a response to every finding, don't replace due diligence, and don't impose fixed contract terms.

questions.stem: Who typically submits the request to bring a new third party into the program?
options: The external auditor who reviews the vendor program each year
The platform administrator, on behalf of every department
The internal business owner or requester who needs the service
The third party's sales representative, through the portal
questions.explanation:
Intake starts with the internal person who wants the service, because they know what it's for and what data it will touch.

Third parties don't initiate their own onboarding, and auditors and admins aren't requesters.

questions.stem: What is the role of the relationship owner (engagement owner) for a third party?
options: They approve their own engagements without any risk review
They configure the questionnaire templates for the whole program
They're accountable for the relationship and its risk in the business
They answer the third party's questionnaires on the vendor's behalf
questions.explanation:
The relationship owner — first line — owns the business relationship, the decision to use the third party, and follow-up on its risks.

Answering for the vendor would destroy independence, and configuration and self-approval belong elsewhere.

questions.stem: An engagement's scope changes: a vendor that only handled marketing now also processes customer payment data. What should happen?
options: Close the engagement and open a new third-party record
Keep the original tier until the next scheduled reassessment
Re-tier the engagement, since its inherent risk has changed
Lower the tier, because the vendor has more experience now
questions.explanation:
Inherent risk follows what the relationship involves. New data types and access mean the tier — and the due diligence it drives — need updating now.

Waiting, lowering the tier, or creating duplicate records all misrepresent the risk.

questions.stem: How should due diligence differ between a tier 1 and a tier 3 engagement?
options: Tier 1 skips due diligence, because critical vendors are pre-approved
Both get the same full questionnaire, so results are always comparable
Tier 3 gets more scrutiny, because low-risk vendors are less mature
Tier 1 gets deeper questionnaires and more evidence; tier 3 gets lighter review
questions.explanation:
A risk-based program scales effort to risk: critical engagements get comprehensive review and evidence, low-risk ones a light touch.

Uniform review wastes effort, and inverting or skipping scrutiny for critical vendors is backwards.

questions.stem: When are onsite assessments most appropriate?
options: Only after a relationship has been offboarded, to confirm the data is gone
For every vendor, regardless of its tier or the service it provides
Only for vendors that refuse to answer any questionnaire you send them
For the most critical third parties, where remote evidence isn't enough
questions.explanation:
Onsite visits are expensive, so they're reserved for the highest-risk relationships where direct observation adds real assurance.

Visiting everyone doesn't scale, refusal is a separate escalation issue, and visiting after offboarding is pointless.

questions.stem: Why do many programs accept standardized questionnaires such as the SIG or CAIQ?
options: Vendors can reuse one standard response, which saves both sides effort
Regulators accept only standardized questionnaires as evidence
Standard questionnaires remove the need to review any vendor answers
Standard questionnaires automatically assign the vendor's tier
questions.explanation:
Industry-standard questionnaires let third parties answer once for many customers, and give you a familiar structure to review.

Answers still need review, regulators accept other evidence, and tiering still comes from your own IRQ.

questions.stem: Which signals are commonly used in continuous monitoring of third parties?
options: Only the vendor's answers from its original onboarding questionnaire
The vendor's social media follower counts and website visitor numbers
The number of emails the vendor sends to your staff each month
Security ratings, financial health, adverse media, and sanctions lists
questions.explanation:
Outside-in signals — security ratings, financial distress, negative news, sanctions — reveal change between assessments.

Popularity and email volume say nothing about risk, and onboarding answers go stale.

questions.stem: What is concentration risk in a third-party program?
options: Too much reliance on one provider, region, or service for critical operations
A questionnaire that concentrates too many questions in one section
A vendor that concentrates its marketing on one industry or customer segment
An assessor who has too many assessments assigned to them at once
questions.explanation:
If many critical services depend on one provider or location, a single failure has outsized impact. Spotting that concentration is a board-level concern.

Marketing focus, questionnaire layout, and workload are unrelated.

questions.stem: An engagement's residual risk is above appetite, but the business wants to proceed. What is appropriate?
options: Let the third party sign off on accepting the risk for you
Proceed quietly and lower the residual rating so it's within appetite
Delete the assessment so the residual risk no longer appears
A formal risk acceptance by an authorized person, with rationale and expiry
questions.explanation:
Proceeding above appetite is a business decision that must be owned, documented, and revisited.

Altering ratings, letting the vendor accept your risk, or deleting evidence all undermine the program.

questions.stem: During offboarding of a vendor that held customer data, what should you obtain?
options: A new full risk assessment of the vendor's current controls
A copy of the vendor's latest marketing brochure
Confirmation that the data was returned or securely destroyed
An invitation for the vendor to join the program again next year
questions.explanation:
Offboarding must close out data risk: data returned or destroyed, ideally with a certificate, alongside access revocation.

A fresh assessment is unnecessary at exit, and invitations or brochures add nothing.

questions.stem: Why is a single, complete third-party inventory important?
options: It replaces the need for any due diligence on the vendors listed
It's only needed for vendors with contracts above $1 million
You can't manage risk from third parties you don't know you have
It lets each department keep its own separate vendor list
questions.explanation:
Unknown vendors — shadow procurement, credit card purchases — can't be tiered or assessed. A complete inventory is the starting point.

Separate departmental lists cause gaps, the inventory doesn't replace due diligence, and small contracts can still carry high risk.

questions.stem: Which metric best shows whether the third-party program is keeping up with risk?
options: The total number of third parties currently in the inventory
The percentage of critical third parties assessed on schedule
The number of questionnaire templates that exist in the program
The number of times third-party contacts log in to the portal
questions.explanation: On-time coverage of critical relationships shows whether the program is doing what matters. Inventory size, template counts, and logins are activity measures, not outcomes.

questions.stem: For a critical provider, why assess its business continuity and disaster recovery?
options: Its outage would disrupt your services, so its recovery capability matters
Continuity is the vendor's concern alone and doesn't affect your risk
Continuity plans are only relevant for vendors that don't store any data
Assessing continuity replaces the need to assess information security
questions.explanation:
If you depend on a provider to deliver critical services, its ability to recover is part of your resilience.

Continuity matters regardless of data, doesn't replace security review, and directly affects you.

questions.stem: A vendor will process personal data on your behalf. What agreement is typically required?
options: A non-compete agreement that stops the vendor working with rivals
No agreement, since the main contract covers personal data automatically
A data processing agreement that sets out obligations for that data
A marketing agreement that covers how the vendor promotes you
questions.explanation:
Privacy laws such as GDPR require a data processing agreement defining what the processor may do with personal data, security obligations, and breach notification.

The other agreements don't address personal data, and it isn't covered automatically.

questions.stem: Under the three lines model, who is accountable day to day for the risk in a specific third-party relationship?
options: The business owner of the relationship (first line)
Internal audit (third line)
The third party's own compliance officer
The third-party risk management team (second line)
questions.explanation:
The business that uses the third party owns the risk. The TPRM function sets the framework and oversees, and internal audit provides independent assurance.

The vendor's compliance officer is accountable for their organization, not yours.

questions.stem: What does a "risk-based approach" mean in third-party risk management?
options: Effort and scrutiny are scaled to the risk each relationship presents
Every third party receives exactly the same level of review each year
Risk is assessed only after a third party has caused an incident
Only the largest vendors by spend are reviewed at all
questions.explanation:
Risk-based means proportionate: more attention where exposure is greater, less where it's low.

Uniform review wastes effort, spend isn't a proxy for risk, and reacting only after incidents isn't management.

questions.stem: Why is a third party's country of operation useful to capture on its record?
options: It sets the third party's inherent risk tier on its own, without an IRQ
It's only used to format the third party's mailing address on letters
It supports sanctions screening, data transfer rules, and concentration views
It determines which portal theme and colors the third party sees when logging in
questions.explanation:
Location drives sanctions checks, cross-border data transfer obligations, and geographic concentration analysis.

It doesn't set portal themes or, by itself, the tier.

questions.stem: Which information belongs on the engagement rather than on the third-party company record?
options: The third party's legal name and its government tax identifier
The third party's parent company and its corporate ownership
The specific service, its business owner, data involved, and dates
The third party's headquarters address and main phone number
questions.explanation: Engagements describe one relationship: what service, who owns it, what data is involved, and when it runs. Legal identity, address, and corporate structure belong on the company record.

questions.stem: Why link engagements to their contracts?
options: So contract terms, renewal dates, and obligations connect to the risk being managed
So the contract can be signed automatically when the assessment closes
So contracts replace the need for engagement records
So the third party can edit contract terms through the portal
questions.explanation:
Linking contracts lets risk teams see audit rights, notification obligations, and renewal dates, and use renewals as reassessment triggers.

It doesn't automate signatures, let vendors edit terms, or replace engagements.

questions.stem: Why relate an engagement to the business applications or services it supports?
options: It shows which business services are affected if the third party fails
It automatically closes incidents on those applications
It lets the third party edit those applications' CMDB records
It removes the need for an inherent risk questionnaire
questions.explanation:
Linking engagements to applications and services connects third-party risk to business impact and operational resilience.

It doesn't grant vendors CMDB access, replace tiering, or close incidents.

questions.stem: An organization has 3,000 vendors in its ERP system. How should they be brought into TPRM?
options: Have assessors type each vendor in by hand from printed reports
Import them through an integration or import set into third-party records
Leave them out until each vendor causes an incident
Ask each vendor to register itself on the portal from scratch
questions.explanation:
Importing from the system of record — with deduplication on a unique identifier — builds the inventory quickly and keeps it aligned.

Manual entry is slow and error-prone, self-registration hands control to vendors, and waiting for incidents defeats the purpose.

questions.stem: How are external security ratings from providers such as BitSight or SecurityScorecard typically brought into TPRM?
options: By assessors copying ratings into the assessment comments by hand
By asking each third party to type its own rating into the portal each month
They can't be brought in; assessors must look them up separately
Through integrations, often from the ServiceNow Store, that update third-party records
questions.explanation:
Risk intelligence integrations pull ratings automatically, so monitoring stays current without manual work.

Self-reported or hand-copied ratings defeat the purpose of independent, continuous signals.

questions.stem: How is a risk intelligence rating usually matched to the right third party?
options: By the date the third party was first added to the program
By the number of engagements the third party currently has
By the name of the internal business owner on the engagement
By identifiers such as the third party's primary domain or company ID
questions.explanation:
Ratings providers track companies by domains and company identifiers, so accurate identifiers on the record are what make matching reliable.

Owner names, dates, and engagement counts don't identify the company.

questions.stem: How does the IRQ determine an engagement's tier?
options: The requester picks whichever tier they prefer
Every engagement starts at tier 1 and moves down yearly
Answers carry scores, and the total maps to tier thresholds
The third party chooses its own tier in the portal
questions.explanation:
IRQ questions are scored, and the resulting score falls into configured tier ranges, so tiering is consistent and explainable.

Letting requesters or vendors choose defeats the control, and fixed starting tiers ignore actual risk.

questions.stem: Risk leadership decides that more engagements should land in tier 1. What should be adjusted?
options: Each engagement's tier, edited one by one after tiering completes
The tier thresholds or question scoring in the tiering configuration
The portal theme, so tier 1 engagements stand out visually
The third parties' security ratings, so more of them look risky
questions.explanation:
Changing thresholds or scoring adjusts how all future tiering works, consistently. Hand-editing tiers bypasses the method.

Themes don't affect tiers, and you can't change external ratings.

questions.stem: Security and privacy questionnaires need different expert reviewers. How should assessments be routed?
options: Assign assessor groups by questionnaire type so each goes to the right experts
Send every assessment to one general mailbox for anyone to pick up
Route all assessments to the platform administrator to triage
Let each third party choose which assessor reviews its responses
questions.explanation:
Routing by type to specialist groups gets responses reviewed by people who understand them.

A shared mailbox loses accountability, vendors shouldn't pick reviewers, and administrators aren't assessors.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of configuring the email notifications sent to third parties?
options: Clear, branded messages that link to the task improve response rates
It lets the third party turn off every reminder they receive from you
It sends third parties a copy of their internal risk score
It replaces the portal, so vendors answer by replying to email
questions.explanation:
Professional, clear notifications with direct links get faster responses and fewer "is this phishing?" questions.

They don't hand control of reminders to vendors, replace the portal, or expose internal scoring.

questions.stem: An internal user adds a new contact for a third party. What generally needs to happen for that contact to use the portal?
options: Nothing is needed; any email address can sign in to the portal directly
An account is created or invited and given the third-party portal role
The contact must be added to an internal IT support group for access
The contact must first be made the primary contact for the company
questions.explanation:
Portal access requires a recognized identity associated with the third party and the portal role.

Internal groups would grant inappropriate access, primary status isn't required, and open access would be insecure.

questions.stem: Why capture the types of data an engagement involves, such as personal or payment data?
options: They decide which portal language the third party will use
They drive tiering and which due-diligence assessments are triggered
They set the third party's contract payment terms
They're only stored for reference and affect nothing
questions.explanation:
Data types are central to inherent risk and determine whether privacy, payment, or other specialized assessments apply.

Language and payment terms are unrelated.

questions.stem: A program needs separate questionnaires for information security, privacy, and business continuity. How should they be set up?
options: As one enormous template that every third party completes in full
As free-text emails that assessors write for each third party
As a single yes/no question asking whether the vendor is secure
As separate questionnaire templates, issued based on tiering and data types
questions.explanation:
Domain-specific templates let the program issue only what applies, keep content maintainable, and route each to the right reviewers.

One giant template wastes effort, emails lose structure, and a single question gives no assurance.

questions.stem: Which question type should collect a third party's SOC 2 report?
options: A yes/no question
A single-line text question
A numeric question
An attachment question
questions.explanation: Attachment questions capture documents directly on the response, keeping evidence with the answer it supports. The other types can't hold a file.

questions.stem: A follow-up question should appear only if the third party says it uses subcontractors. What feature supports this?
options: Conditional questions that depend on an earlier answer
An assessor manually deleting the question afterward
A note asking vendors to skip the question if needed
A separate questionnaire sent to every third party
questions.explanation:
Conditional (dependent) questions show follow-ups only when relevant, keeping questionnaires short and focused.

Separate questionnaires, notes, and manual deletion are clumsy workarounds.

questions.stem: How are a respondent's answers turned into a score?
options: The assessor guesses a score after reading the whole response
Each answer option maps to a score value, weighted and combined
Scores are based on how quickly the questionnaire was completed
The third party enters its own score at the end of the form
questions.explanation:
Configured scores for each answer, combined with weights, produce consistent, explainable results.

Guessing, self-scoring, and speed aren't valid scoring methods.

questions.stem: Some questions must always be answered before a questionnaire can be submitted. How is this enforced?
options: By giving those questions a higher weight
By placing those questions first on the form
By making those questions conditional
By marking those questions as mandatory
questions.explanation: Mandatory questions block submission until answered. Weight affects scoring, order affects layout, and conditional logic affects visibility.

questions.stem: Third parties often miss assessment deadlines. What configuration helps most?
options: Removing due dates entirely so third parties never feel rushed
Closing each assessment the moment its due date has passed
Letting each third party choose its own due date for responses
Due dates with automated reminders before and after the deadline
questions.explanation:
Clear deadlines plus reminders keep assessments moving without punishing vendors for small delays.

Removing or vendor-controlled deadlines lose control, and instant closure wastes work.

questions.stem: An assessor goes on leave with several assessments under review. What should happen?
options: Leave them assigned to the absent assessor until they come back
Reassign the assessments to another assessor so reviews continue
Cancel them all and reissue them to the third parties from scratch
Close them as complete using the answers that were already submitted
questions.explanation:
Reassignment keeps work moving without disturbing the third party or losing review progress.

Waiting delays risk decisions, cancelling wastes the vendor's effort, and closing without review skips the control.

questions.stem: While reviewing, an assessor finds one answer unclear. What's the best action?
options: Ignore the question and score the rest
Request more information on that question from the third party
Score the question as a failure without asking
Change the third party's answer to what seems likely
questions.explanation:
Asking for clarification on the specific question keeps the record accurate and fair.

Failing it unasked, editing the vendor's answer, or ignoring it all compromise the assessment.

questions.stem: A program wants an issue raised automatically whenever a vendor says it doesn't encrypt data at rest. How is this done?
options: Add a note to the question telling vendors to raise their own issue
Configure an issue rule on that question and answer combination
Ask assessors to remember to raise one each time they see it
Lower the question's weight so the answer doesn't affect the score
questions.explanation: Rules tied to specific responses make issue creation consistent. Relying on memory or vendors misses findings, and lowering weight hides them.

questions.stem: What does a completed due-diligence assessment typically contribute to an engagement?
options: A new third-party company record
A signed contract between the parties
A residual risk rating based on the assessed controls
A new inherent risk tier that replaces the IRQ result
questions.explanation: Assessment results reflect the control environment and feed residual risk. Inherent risk comes from tiering, contracts are separate, and the company record already exists.

questions.stem: Which events should trigger an out-of-cycle reassessment?
options: The third party changing its logo or redesigning its public website
A contract renewal, a vendor breach, a scope change, or a ratings drop
A new employee joining the internal business owner's team
The assessor's own annual performance review being completed
questions.explanation: Reassessment triggers are events that change the risk picture. Branding changes and internal staffing changes don't.

questions.stem: A program wants to use the industry-standard SIG questionnaire. What's the advantage?
options: SIG answers never need to be reviewed by an assessor once they're submitted
SIG questionnaires don't need to be scored, because they're industry standard
Using the SIG removes the need for tiering, since it covers every vendor
Vendors may already have answers, and the content is widely understood
questions.explanation: Standard content speeds responses and gives assessors a familiar structure. Responses still need review and scoring, and tiering still determines scope.

questions.stem: A third party uploads a SOC 2 report covering last calendar year. Why track the report's coverage period?
options: Reports older than a week can't be read by assessors
The platform deletes reports when they're a year old
Evidence ages, so you know when to request an updated report
The coverage period determines the vendor's tier
questions.explanation:
Assurance reports cover a specific period. Tracking it shows when evidence is stale and a new report — or a bridge letter — is needed.

It doesn't affect readability or tiering, and reports aren't deleted automatically.

questions.stem: A vendor's SOC 2 report ended in June, and the next one won't be ready until March. What can the vendor provide to cover the gap?
options: Nothing; gaps between reports can't be covered
A bridge letter stating no material control changes since the report period
A copy of its marketing brochure describing its security features
An email from its sales team saying everything is fine
questions.explanation:
Bridge (gap) letters are management assertions covering the period between the report's end and the present. They're weaker than an audited report but standard practice.

Marketing material and sales emails aren't assurance.

questions.stem: How can an assessment address fourth-party risk?
options: Assume subcontractors are covered by the vendor's own insurance policy
Ignore subcontractors, since you have no contract with them
Send your questionnaire directly to every subcontractor without the vendor knowing
Include questions about the vendor's critical subcontractors and how it oversees them
questions.explanation:
Asking your third party who its critical subcontractors are and how it manages them gives visibility without contracting with them directly.

Bypassing the vendor, relying on insurance, or ignoring subcontractors leaves gaps.

questions.stem: Why keep previous assessments rather than overwriting them?
options: Because old assessments set the tier for the next year
Because the platform can't create a new assessment otherwise
So the third party can reuse old answers without reviewing them
To compare results over time and show whether a vendor is improving
questions.explanation:
History shows trends, supports audits, and helps assessors focus on what changed.

New assessments don't depend on old ones, answers should be reviewed, and tiering comes from the IRQ.

questions.stem: A question doesn't apply to a particular third party. How should the vendor respond?
options: Leave it blank and hope the assessor doesn't notice it was skipped
Mark it not applicable, with a short justification for the assessor
Delete the question from the questionnaire before submitting the response
Answer "yes" so that the overall score isn't affected by the question
questions.explanation:
A justified not-applicable answer is honest and reviewable, and scoring can exclude it.

Blank or false answers undermine the assessment, and respondents can't edit the template.

questions.stem: An engagement is cancelled before its assessment is finished. What should happen to the assessment?
options: Delete it so it doesn't appear in any reports
Close it complete with the answers submitted so far
Leave it open in case the engagement starts again
Close it incomplete so it stops but its record is kept
questions.explanation:
Closing incomplete records why the work stopped without implying a finished result.

Leaving it open creates noise, deleting loses the record, and closing complete misrepresents it.

questions.stem: How are assessment scores typically translated into ratings such as low, medium, and high?
options: Assessors pick a rating based on their impression
Third parties choose the rating that fits their score
Ratings are assigned in rotation across vendors
Score ranges are mapped to ratings in the configuration
questions.explanation:
Configured score ranges make ratings consistent and explainable across all assessments.

Impressions, self-selection, and rotation aren't valid methods.

questions.stem: An engagement has security, privacy, and continuity assessments. How do they relate to its overall result?
options: The assessment with the lowest score is ignored as an outlier
Each produces results that together inform the engagement's residual risk
Only the first assessment completed counts toward the result
They must be merged into a single questionnaire after submission
questions.explanation:
Each domain contributes to the overall picture of the relationship. Ignoring any of them would hide risk.

Order of completion doesn't matter, outliers aren't discarded, and merging isn't needed.

questions.stem: Several people at a third party contribute to one questionnaire. How can they coordinate before submitting?
options: They email answers to the assessor, who enters them on their behalf
Collaborate on the saved draft, with sections delegated, before final submission
Only one person can ever see the questionnaire at a time
Each person submits their own copy, and the assessor merges them
questions.explanation:
Saved drafts and delegation let several contacts contribute, and one submission keeps the response coherent.

Multiple submissions or assessor data entry create confusion and break attribution.

questions.stem: How can an assessor ask a third party a question about a specific response?
options: Call the vendor on the phone and keep no record of what was discussed
Edit the question text itself so that it includes the follow-up question
Use comments on the response so the conversation stays on the record
Send a text message to the vendor contact's personal mobile phone
questions.explanation:
Comments on the response keep the exchange attached to the evidence, visible to both sides, and auditable.

Unrecorded calls, personal texts, and edited questions lose the trail.

questions.stem: An internal team performs an onsite visit to a critical vendor. How should the results be recorded?
options: They don't need to be recorded, as long as the visit found nothing of concern
As a free-text comment added to the third party's company record afterward
As an assessment completed by the internal team and linked to the engagement
In a private notebook that the visiting assessor keeps for their own reference
questions.explanation:
Recording the visit as an assessment keeps results structured, scored, and linked to the engagement and its risk.

Private notes and comments aren't structured evidence, and clean results still need recording.

questions.stem: What typically triggers a privacy assessment for an engagement?
options: The third party's headquarters being in the same country
IRQ answers showing the third party will process personal data
The third party having a website privacy policy
The engagement's contract value exceeding a threshold
questions.explanation:
Processing personal data is what creates privacy risk, so IRQ answers about it trigger the privacy assessment.

Having a privacy policy, spend, or location alone don't determine whether privacy review applies.

questions.stem: Why use the same questionnaire template across similar third parties?
options: Results are comparable, which makes portfolio reporting meaningful
It means assessors no longer need to review the answers
It's required before a third party can log in to the portal
It lets every third party skip questions that don't suit them
questions.explanation:
Consistent templates produce comparable scores and findings across vendors.

Templates don't let vendors skip questions, remove review, or affect portal access.
